newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Naphtha/Mogas - Naphtha firms amid KPC talks.
newsitem.headline: Asia Naphtha/Mogas - Naphtha firms amid KPC talks.

text.p: Naphtha firmed despite softer crude while gasoline extended its losses amid aggressive trader selling, traders said on Thursday.
Traders however assessed supplies as balanced to tight with Singapore production down amid two refinery scheduled shutdowns in March.
The Singapore Refining Co shut down a 14,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) hydrocracker February 18 for 10 days, reducing supplies of distillates.
An Australian refiner also shutdown a 23,000-bpd fluid catalytic cracker February 21 for two to three weeks, but is not expected to have any requirements, industry sources said.
But shutdowns of toppers and reformers in May at Mobil's two refineries in Altona and Adelaide is likely to prompt imports into Australia, probably from Singapore, traders said.
In the Singapore fob market, a Dutch trader emerged to offer 95-octane unleaded gasoline lifting in March at $27.20 per barrel.
Unleaded 92-octane was traded between a Japanese trader and a Singapore trader at $26.40 per barrel for March 17-21, marginally firmer from Wednesday's trade at $26.35.
Traders said a Dutch trader and a South Korean refiner won Taiwan's reformate tender at $27.90 and $28.20 per barrel c-and-f Taiwan respectively.
Taiwan's tender for 250,000-barrel cargoes of 95-octane unleaded reformate for March 16-30 delivery closed February 18 and was valid for two days.
Naphtha prices in turn extended their gains in a tight market.
March naphtha swaps were last quoted at $24.10/$24.15 per barrel, up from $23.90/$24.10 on Wednesday.

Although trade was thin as north Asian buyers had already covered March needs and have yet to enter the market for April. Sentiment was bullish, spurring record high premiums in talks for Kuwaiti term naphtha with its Asian buyers.

Traders said talks for over two million tonnes of full range naphtha were in a wide-range, of $12 to $16 per tonne over Mideast naptha fob spot quotes, much higher than Kuwait's price for August 1996-September 1997 of $7.90.
But the high price was not deterring any buyers from renewing contracts and some were even asking for an increase in volume.
"In fact, some parties want to increase volumes because naphtha is so tight, especially for such full range naphtha," said a Japanese trader.
Kuwaiti sources said term contracts will only be finalised next week.
(Prices are in dollars per barrel)
